Quand j’ai rencontré Chris, je ne connai: When I met Chris, I didn’t know much about the world of boxing. I became interested because of the wave of hate that hit Olympic champion Imane Khelif (before she actually became champion). The story reminded me of another one, that of Serena Williams, who was long criticized for having a “man’s” physique and strength. I remembered the stories of many Mediterranean women around me who were told they were too tall, too hairy, too strong, too good at sports. As if femininity were a single model, set in stone. Often, these women are racialized and dare to assert themselves, excel professionally or… win an Olympic medal.
Chris, lui, est un boxeur amateur de lon: Chris, for his part, has been an amateur boxer for a long time. After a few minutes of conversation, it’s clear that he knows the field inside out and, above all, that he is passionate about it. He is also an experienced journalist who very generously agreed to introduce me to the sport and to be my mentor for this article, which we co-wrote. I was able to join him for interviews with inspiring young women boxers. He also shared with me his admiration for these young women who push past every prejudice to become excellent boxers.
Trouver des boxeuses racisées n’a pas ét: Finding racialized women boxers wasn’t so easy. We called and visited several clubs, including Barbu Kickboxing and Académie martiale Ness, which put us in touch with Aya, a 22-year-old boxer of Algerian origin, and Luxia, a 19-year-old boxer of African descent. Both women impressed us with their passion, their discipline and their positive outlook.
J’ai beaucoup appris dans cet exercice à: I learned a lot from working as a pair. I hope you will enjoy reading the article, and find it as interesting, as much as I enjoyed writing it and discovering this sport.

La polémique sur la féminité de la champ: The controversy over the femininity of Algerian Olympic champion Imane Khelif has echoed even among some racialized women boxers in Montréal. But it only strengthens their determination to become better boxers.
En croisant Aya Ahmed Lechheb dans la ru: Passing Aya Ahmed Lechheb on the street, you would never guess she is a boxer. Outside the gym, Aya is rather reserved. The 22-year-old respiratory therapist stands a little over 1.5 metres tall, blushes easily and lives in Montréal’s Saint-Michel neighbourhood with her parents and her little sister. Five nights a week, she works herself hard in the basement of a church on Jarry Street. Since February, Aya has devoted herself entirely to kickboxing.
Certains soirs, elle se rend au gymnase: Some nights, she gets to the gym at 6 p.m., warms up for 20 minutes, does drills for two hours, then spends 45 minutes sparring against men twice her size. When she has drained her body, she takes the bus home and, if she’s lucky, manages to sleep five hours before waking at dawn to start her shift at the hospital.
« Quand je suis au gym, je n'ai pas le t: “When I’m at the gym, I don’t have time to think about work or what’s going on in my head. When I’m here, I only do kickboxing,” says Aya, as she gets ready for her training session at Barbu Kickboxing.
« Travailler dans un hôpital est parfois: “Working in a hospital is sometimes especially stressful, but training and fighting help me control my emotions better. Taking hits and continuing anyway has an enormous impact on my life. Even though I’m not the best athlete in the club. This discipline changes the way I see myself,” she says.
Depuis ses études supérieures, la boxeus: Since her university studies, the boxer has worn a hijab, which sometimes draws critical looks. Like the evening when, as she was walking home, a stranger screamed insults at her about her headscarf. It was not the first, nor the last, attack targeting her choice of clothing.
Aya estime que le kickboxing lui évite d: Aya says kickboxing keeps her from feeling helpless when she walks down a dark street. “I don’t have much self-esteem, but that has changed since I started training, especially when I walk alone on the street. I’m not She-Hulk, but I feel safer when I’m outside,” the athlete confides.
En tant que boxeuse amatrice originaire: As an amateur boxer originally from Algeria, she naturally had her eyes glued to the television last Friday, during the bout in which Imane Khelif won gold at the Paris Olympic Games. She had tears in her eyes as the Algerian boxer was on her way to beating her Chinese opponent, Yang Liu.
« Le présentateur pleurait, je pleurais,: “The announcer was crying, I was crying, my mother was crying too and my father had tears in his eyes. I don’t think I’ve ever seen him cry!” Aya exclaims.
Comme beaucoup, Aya n'a découvert l’olym: Like many people, Aya only discovered the Algerian Olympian after the flood of hateful online messages, death threats and false accusations of cheating against her. Imane Khelif, 25, found herself in the middle of a media storm after her victory over Angela Carini by technical knockout. Her Italian opponent abandoned the fight after only 47 seconds, complaining she had never been hit so hard. Statements made by the Carini camp also fuelled speculation that Imane Khelif was in fact a man fighting women.
Ces affirmations ont été amplifiées par: These claims were amplified by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, billionaire Elon Musk, owner of the social network X (formerly Twitter), J.K. Rowling (author of the Harry Potter series), former U.S. president Donald Trump and a whole panel of public figures eager to go after an amateur boxer they had never heard of before. While the lies about Imane Khelif’s gender and sex set social media ablaze, Aya wasn’t fooled so easily.
« Faites vos recherches, l'Algérie n'env: “Do your research, Algeria would not send a trans boxer to the Olympic Games, it makes no sense,” says Aya, who lived in her country of origin until the age of 6. “I feel like there is progress over time, but there’s still a long way to go. We all need to learn more about each other.”
Mais cette campagne de dénigrement a tou: But the smear campaign still had an effect on Montréal’s combat sports scene. Gym owners, event promoters and well-known athletes shared memes that photoshopped an Adam’s apple onto Imane Khelif, a bulge in her pants, or used words like “disgusting” and “monster” to describe the Olympic champion.
« À ce stade, on se demande si on on sim: “At this point, you wonder whether we even have the right to exist. Can we be women who do this sport? If she [Imane Khelif] is too strong, it must be because she’s a man or she’s on steroids. If I wear a hijab, it’s because I’m weak and need to be saved. It’s so heavy, sometimes,” says Imane wryly.
La polémique sur la féminité d’Imane Khe: The controversy over Imane Khelif’s femininity stems from a test that reportedly revealed the presence of male chromosomes in the boxer at the International Boxing Association (IBA) championships in 2023.
Or, l'IBA, basée en Russie, n'a jamais p: However, the Russia-based IBA never published the results and has given conflicting accounts of the test it carried out and of the results it obtained.
Néanmoins, cette année-là Imane Khelif a: Nevertheless, that year Imane Khelif was disqualified just three days after her victory over Russian hopeful Azalia Amideva, without the Algerian being given the opportunity to appeal the decision. Taiwanese boxer Lin Yu-ting was also barred for failing an unspecified sex test at the IBA championships, after beating a Bulgarian boxer.
Dans les deux cas, les athlètes sont acc: In both cases, the athletes are accused of having XY chromosomes or high levels of testosterone in their bodies. These allegations have never been independently verified. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) no longer recognizes the IBA’s authority over boxing because of its ties to the Putin regime and its financial opacity. When the IOC took over Olympic boxing ahead of the Paris Games, it determined that Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting were eligible to compete.
La semaine dernière, l'IBA a été contrai: Last week, the IBA was forced to admit that it had tested only four women out of the hundreds who took part in the 2023 championships. The organization also acknowledged that these tests were carried out only after complaints from opposing athletes, thereby injecting bias into what should be an impartial process.
« Quand on voit une organisation avec la: “When you see an organization with ‘International’ in its name, you assume it’s legitimate, but when you look more closely, the picture becomes much murkier,” observes Morgan Campbell, a sports journalist who covered the Olympic Games for Radio-Canada and provides colourful commentary on boxing events across Canada.
« L'IBA n'est plus reconnue par le CIO e: “The IBA is no longer recognized by the IOC because of deep, long-standing corruption. You don’t suddenly give a femininity test in the middle of a tournament. You test athletes before the competition and you determine whether those people are eliminated. That’s how international boxing works. Because if these accusations are well-founded, it means the IBA allowed these athletes to endanger their fellow competitors all the way to the championship rounds, and only then decided to run tests? So even if they have the appearance of authenticity, these tests are just as specious as a passerby on the street saying: ‘Hey, that girl is too tall to be a woman, she must be a guy!’” the sports journalist explains.
Comme Morgan Campbell et d'autres expert: As Morgan Campbell and other experts point out, the recent string of “gender doping” allegations has been levelled almost exclusively against women of colour or women who do not conform to Western standards of beauty.
Après avoir remporté le 800 mètres aux c: After winning the 800 metres at the 2009 world championships, South African Caster Semenya saw the rules governing the discipline changed to exclude her. She was designated female at birth, was raised as a girl and has always identified as a woman. But she was born with an intersex condition that produces natural testosterone levels higher than those of most women.
Lorsque World Athletics (l'instance diri: When World Athletics (the governing body of track and field) changed the rules in 2011, it required women competing in the 400, 800 and 1,500 metres to undergo gender testing and to suppress their natural testosterone if it exceeded the “female range.” At first, these requirements were not added to the 100- and 200-metre races. “They literally changed the rules for the events Caster Semenya runs. It’s hard not to feel like she was targeted,” says Morgan Campbell.
Aujourd'hui, plus de dix ans plus tard,: Today, more than ten years later, the South African athlete is still engaged in a legal battle with World Athletics over her classification as a woman. Indian sprinter Dutee Chand, African-American basketball star Brittney Griner and Indian middle-distance runner Santhi Soundarajan have also all been accused of gender doping.
Bien que la plupart des critiques initia: Although most of the initial criticism of Imane Khelif wrongly accused her of being a trans woman, the IBA has since claimed that she has a condition similar to Caster Semenya’s. The boxing association has provided no evidence to support these claims.
Les débats sur le sexe des athlètes ont: Debates over athletes’ sex have resurfaced in recent years, but the first femininity test in international sports competition dates back to the Cold War.
C’est parce que les femmes de l'Union so: It was because women from the Soviet Union began to dominate the Olympic Games that Western sports authorities decided these athletes <l1>were not women</l1>. In 1966, the International Association of Athletics Federations therefore introduced a “nude parade” in which officials inspected each athlete before she took part in the competition.
Selon le journaliste Morgan Campbell, bi: According to journalist Morgan Campbell, although Imane Khelif competed at the Tokyo Olympics and in countless other international tournaments, the “gender doping” allegations were only made once she improved her boxing performances at the IBA championships.
« Vous voulez savoir ce qui a changé che: “Do you want to know what changed about Imane Khelif since her loss at the Tokyo Olympics? Algeria hired one of the best boxing coaches in the world to work on her game. It’s Pedro Diaz, who comes from Cuba. In the 1990s, he trained teams that piled up gold medals at the Olympic Games. He has worked with world champions like Miguel Cotto and Guillermo Rigondeaux. He’s the real deal. He’s a genius,” says Campbell. “Although Imane Khelif competed at the Tokyo Olympics and in countless other international tournaments, the ‘gender doping’ allegations were only made once she improved her boxing performances at the IBA championships,” he adds.
« Imane Khelif ne s'est pas soudainement: “Imane Khelif didn’t suddenly turn into a man between 2021 and today. The Algerian federation hired a brilliant boxing coach who knew how to bring out the best in her, who showed her how to use her tools.”
La championne algérienne est plus grande: The Algerian champion is taller and more muscular than most of her opponents in the Olympic boxing tournament. The gold medal bout against Yang Liu neutralized those advantages. And that was clear from the start of the fight. Used to moving in and out of her opponents’ range while landing long-distance punches, Imane Khelif needed most of the first round before she began to connect with Yang Liu.
Mais malgré ces difficultés initiales, I: But despite these early difficulties, Imane Khelif managed to disrupt Yang Liu’s rhythm, push her back onto the ropes and land her famous cross. She also fended off Yang Liu’s attacks by slipping around them and using the Chinese boxer’s momentum to land powerful counterpunches. By amateur boxing standards, it was a very technical and very clean bout.
Contrairement à la boxe professionnelle,: Unlike professional boxing, which can go 12 rounds at the championship level, amateur bouts last only three rounds of three minutes. Fighters who rely on power alone tend to be mediocre in this Olympic sport, which emphasizes footwork, defence and volume over damage inflicted.
Les règles du sport amateur tendent à fa: The rules of the amateur sport tend to favour bigger, sturdier fighters who score from the outside and stay out of their opponents’ reach (two things Imane Khelif did brilliantly throughout the Olympic Games). “Imane doesn’t have a man’s body, she has the body of an elite amateur boxer,” Morgan Campbell explains. “Nobody complains when that happens in men’s boxing,” he concludes.
Le plus grand inconvénient de la controv: The biggest downside of the Khelif controversy may be the effect it could have on amateur women’s boxing, a sport that made its first appearance at the Olympic Games just 12 years ago. While the arrival of women’s boxing at the Olympics has fuelled the careers of professional champions such as Clarissa Shields, Katie Taylor and Lauren Price, its growth has been slow in Canada and Quebec.
Le Québec est la plaque tournante de la: Quebec is the hub of Canadian amateur boxing – nearly half the members of the national amateur team come from the province – but few women and girls take part in competitions at the amateur level. “When we go abroad to compete, the young women are always amazed at how advanced the amateur programs are in European countries,” says Kenneth Piché, executive director of the Fédération québécoise de boxe.
« Nous avons environ 1 600 boxeurs inscr: “We have about 1,600 registered boxers, and maybe 20% of them are women of different ages and weight classes. So it’s not always easy to find them opponents with comparable experience in the same weight class,” the director explains. “And in amateur competition, you can’t move up to more competitive events if you don’t have enough experience. So it’s not easy, but we’re working on it,” the executive director of the Fédération québécoise de boxe assures.

For this 19-year-old, who describes herself as “stubborn,” fitting in hasn’t always been easy. “I was often the only Black girl in my class, but my parents encouraged me to be the best,” she explains. “They would tell me, ‘Okay, you’re the only Black girl. So what? If others can do it, you can do it too.’ In soccer, which was my first sport, I had to be the best to stand out. I was the only Black player, the only francophone. It pushed me to improve and to earn my teammates’ respect,” she says.
Quand elle découvre la boxe, c’est le co: When she discovered boxing, it was love at first sight. In the ring, she experiences the present moment: it’s just her and her opponent. “When I box, I feel powerful, I’m proud, I want to give everything I have,” she says. “What I love is the discipline it teaches you. It’s not just a physical activity. You have to train your mind, improve your technique, learn to breathe and to take hits. All of that takes training,” the athlete explains.
Luxia avoue qu'elle n'a pas de modèles q: Luxia admits she has no role models who look like her in Quebec’s boxing world. She has found inspiration in other sports, such as tennis. “Serena Williams experienced a lot of racism. She was also accused of being a man and of being too strong for a woman. And yet she carved out this incredible path thanks to her mental strength, her intelligence and her determination. That inspires me,” she confides.
Imane Khelif serait née avec un avantage: Imane Khelif is said to have been born with a genetic advantage over her competitors. Some experts believe sport punishes her and other women athletes while celebrating those same advantages in men. In the case of Olympic gold medallist Michael Phelps, researchers found that his body produced half as much lactic acid as his competitors’, allowing him to recover quickly and endure longer training sessions. Michael Phelps also has an unusually long torso, double-jointed elbows and short legs, which lets him glide through the water more efficiently than most swimmers. “Nobody says Michael Phelps doesn’t train hard or doesn’t deserve his results, but he was born with these enormous advantages,” notes journalist Morgan Campbell. “That’s sport.”
